name: Mempool
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: The Waiting Room: How Transactions Queue for a Block
lesson.summary: The mempool is the holding area where a node keeps transactions it has heard about but that have not yet been confirmed in a block, and it is where a real fee market plays out in public.
lesson.body:
Between the moment you broadcast a transaction and the moment it lands inside a block body, it has to sit somewhere. That somewhere is the mempool, short for memory pool: a working list, held in the memory of a node, of transactions that look valid but have not yet been included in the chain. Every node defined back in the Node chapter that relays transactions keeps one of its own, and it is constantly being added to as new transactions arrive over the peer to peer network, and trimmed as blocks confirm some of them and remove them from the queue.

A detail that surprises a lot of newcomers is that there is no single, official mempool shared by the whole network. Each node builds its own view based on which transactions it happened to receive, in what order, and under what relay policy it enforces, such as a minimum fee rate it is willing to pass along. Two honest nodes on opposite sides of the world can have mempools that differ by dozens of transactions at any given moment simply because propagation across a large peer to peer network takes time and does not follow one guaranteed path.

The mempool is also where blockspace scarcity becomes visible. A block body has a limited amount of room, so when more transactions are waiting than can fit in the next few blocks, they effectively compete for inclusion. Miners and validators, who are economically motivated, tend to pick transactions offering the highest fee per byte first, since that is how they maximize their own reward from producing a block. During a period of high demand, someone who wants fast inclusion has to outbid everyone else waiting in the same queue, and someone attaching a very low fee might sit in the mempool for hours or get dropped entirely once nodes decide it is too old or too cheap to keep around.

A concrete example makes this tangible. Imagine a network where a block can fit roughly two thousand average sized transactions and a new block appears about every ten minutes. If eight thousand transactions are sitting in the mempool at once, only the highest paying quarter of them will make it into the very next block, and the rest keep waiting, watching new arrivals with higher fees jump the queue ahead of them. This is exactly why wallets often let a user pick a fee, and why that fee is really a bid for a scarce resource rather than a fixed cost.

None of this changes what makes a transaction valid in the first place, since a transaction still has to pass the same signature and balance checks described in the Transaction chapter before a node will even accept it into its mempool. What the mempool adds is timing and priority: it is the visible, if slightly inconsistent, staging ground where the network's raw demand for confirmation meets the limited supply of space inside each new block body.
